title: Candlemas (2 February)
hook: forty days after Christmas: Simeon's light, and candles blessed
carry: a light to lighten the gentiles

segments.voice: Yesterday, St Brigid and a cross woven from floor rushes. Your line was spring is coming. What sign of it did you find? Day one thousand nineteen.

Two small birds. That's the offering a young couple come to the temple in Jerusalem to make, along with their baby. The law in Leviticus says that after the birth of a son the mother waits seven days, then thirty-three more, and then brings an offering: a lamb, or, if she can't afford a lamb, two turtledoves or two young pigeons. Mary and Joseph come with the birds' offering. In the crowded courts, one man has been waiting for something only he knows about. Churches keep this day in early February, counting from Christmas, and in some churches it begins with candles. Today's word is what the couple came to do.

Luke tells it like this, in the King James Bible: "And when the days of her purification according to the law of Moses were accomplished, they brought him to Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord." That's the Presentation: a firstborn son brought to the temple and offered back to God, the way the law asks. A family doing what faithful families did. Then Simeon. Luke says he was just and devout, and that the Holy Ghost had shown him he would not see death before he had seen the Lord's Christ. So he has been waiting, scanning faces. And when this couple with their two birds walks in, he knows. He takes the baby in his arms, blesses God, and says words that some churches still sing at the close of the day: "Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word: For mine eyes have seen thy salvation, Which thou hast prepared before the face of all people; A light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel." See what Simeon is holding: a baby who hasn't said a word. And he calls him light, for his own people and for everyone outside them. Light sits at the heart of the English name for the day, Candlemas. In some churches candles are blessed and carried in procession, lit against the February dark, in some places the candles for the year ahead. Orthodox Christians call the feast the Meeting, because the old man and the child meet. Catholics and Anglicans often call it the Presentation. However it's named, Simeon's part of the story ends with a man at peace, ready to go, because he got to hold the light before he left.

Here's the practice: light a candle, if you have one, or switch on one small lamp in a dim room. Settle, and breathe. Look at the flame for a while. Think of something you've waited a long time to see, and whether it came. If you pray, you can say Simeon's words slowly: Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word. If you don't, simply sit with the light and let your shoulders drop, the way someone does when a long wait is over. The bell holds the time.
Presentation. The baby brought to the temple and offered to God, where Simeon took him in his arms and called him a light.
Your line: a light to lighten the gentiles. Today, notice someone standing at the edge of a group near you, and draw them in. Day one thousand nineteen.

howItsDone: At Candlemas, Catholic, Anglican and some Lutheran churches bless candles and carry them in procession; Orthodox churches keep the same feast as the Meeting of the Lord, and Simeon's song is sung at evening prayer in several traditions.

original.note: Greek: light. Simeon calls the child φῶς, a light to lighten the Gentiles (Luke 2:32).

trapdoor: what you thought: a day about candles.
what it means: the baby presented in the temple, and a man who calls him light and is ready to die in peace.
what a scholar hears: Luke 2:22–32 — the purification law of Leviticus 12 kept by a family bringing the birds' offering, and Simeon's song, the Nunc Dimittis.

notes: Claims rule: the 'forty days' of the index hook is given only as Leviticus 12's own count (seven days, then thirty-three), and the feast is said to fall 'in early February, counting from Christmas'.
'Maybe for years' for Simeon's wait is soft speculation; Luke gives no length. Confirm or cut.
'Churches still sing at the close of the day' and 'in some churches' candles are blessed: kept soft per the claims rule; confirm.
Names of the feast: Meeting (Orthodox), Presentation (Catholic/Anglican), Candlemas (English); confirm.

Editor: Luke does not call Simeon old or say how long he waited, so 'old man', 'a very long time' and 'maybe for years' are cut; Leviticus 12's seven-plus-thirty-three days now tied to the birth of a son; candles 'used through the year' and the 'poorest offering' superlative softened; carry changed so it no longer echoes day 1008's 'carry a little light'.

Editor 2: Luke does not call Simeon old, so 'old man' cut from the hook screen and trapdoor; Luke does not say the family was poor or could only afford birds, so fork reveal and trapdoor softened; 'churches still sing' and 'Christians keep' made less sweeping; 'can't yet lift his head' (an age inference) replaced.

Audit: Luke 2:36-38 has Anna the prophetess also recognize the child, so 'nobody looks twice... except one man' cut; 'a cage' and 'carry up the steps' (not in Luke) dropped; 'the story ends' narrowed to Simeon's part (Luke continues with Simeon's word to Mary and Anna).
